paragraphs: The day often starts with sorting and loading at a local station. Couriers then follow routes for pickups and deliveries, coordinating access or refusals on site. They take detours to protect delivery times, complete missed signatures and returns in the afternoon, and submit proof of delivery and exception reports before the next shift is planned.

In one sentence: deliver each item on time. The work includes pickup, route planning, delivery, signatures, exception handling, and proof-of-delivery submission. It requires physical effort and judgment at the last mile.

The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) reports that about 247,200 couriers and messengers were employed in 2024. Employment is projected to reach 267,600 by 2034, a net gain of about 20,400 jobs, with roughly 27,900 openings each year. The median annual wage was about $38,300 in 2026 (BLS OOH, 2026).

AI will not replace last-mile courier work, but it will reduce its premium. Systems now handle dispatch and route planning, shifting the job from finding routes independently to efficient execution, exception handling, and customer service. Pure volume-based manual work faces the most pressure. Couriers who provide good service and resolve problems have more staying power.

paragraphs: The biggest career risk is not AI alone, but the combination of algorithms and outsourcing. Platforms compress last-mile labor costs, while couriers with stronger service skills remain more resilient.

The main risks are algorithmic dispatch and contract outsourcing. Platforms assign routes and prices through systems, putting downward pressure on last-mile labor costs. Traffic accidents and customer complaints also create material pressure.

No matter how capable the system becomes, people still clear access controls, handle delivery refusals, prioritize urgent items, and obtain signatures. Human work remains essential at the last mile. This is career exploration guidance, not a guarantee of employment or a hiring decision.
The market needs fewer people who simply move fast and more dependable courier specialists who know their routes, serve customers well, and stay composed.

In one sentence: deliver each item on time. The work includes pickup, route planning, delivery, signatures, exception handling, and proof-of-delivery submission. It requires physical effort and judgment at the last mile.

Couriers handle last-mile pickup, delivery, and in-person signatures, so their focus is fulfillment. Warehouse workers receive, sort, and store goods, so their focus is inventory. One works outside; the other works mainly in a warehouse.

AI will not replace the job as a whole, but it will reduce its premium. Systems take over dispatch and routing, while couriers focus on efficient execution, exception handling, and customer service. People who handle problems and customers well are more resilient than those who compete only on delivery volume.
Access coordination, communication about refused deliveries, on-site exception handling, and the service judgment needed to deliver urgent items safely.

The work suits people with a strong sense of direction who are punctual, resilient, and comfortable with physical demands. A good courier balances physical work with service and treats on-time delivery as the standard.

Most roles are on last-mile routes for courier stations, e-commerce companies, and on-demand delivery platforms. Work combines outdoor delivery with time-sensitive station shifts organized by neighborhood.

It can be worthwhile if you choose the right direction. Pure volume work is shrinking, but people with strong neighborhood knowledge, low complaint rates, and exception-handling skills still have room to grow. Station management, dispatch, and contracted outlet operations offer broader paths.
